rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening letters are treated in the commentary’s earlier discussion of the sūra openings; the Book is the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: تقدم القول في فواتح السور، والكتاب القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation calls the Book clear because it lays out rulings, including lawful and forbidden matters.
rows.anchor: من جهة أحكامه وحلاله وحرامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation makes its clarity consist in its exhortations, guidance, and light.
rows.anchor: من جهة مواعظه وهداه ونوره

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: A reported view locates the Qur’an’s clarity in Arabic expression, said to contain six letters not combined in another tongue.
rows.anchor: روي هذا القول عن معاذ بن جبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further possibility is that the Qur’an makes Muhammad’s prophethood clear through its inimitability.
rows.anchor: مبينا لنبوة محمد بإعجازه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers all the proposed senses together: the Book is clear in every one of these ways.
rows.anchor: والصواب أنه «مبين» بجميع هذه الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “We sent it down” refers to the Book; sending down can mean establishing it or describe its recitation and wording.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله: أنزلناه ل الكتاب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj takes the pronoun to mean the account of Joseph; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: الضمير في أنزلناه يراد به خبر يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects al-Zajjāj’s interpretation of the pronoun as Joseph’s story as weak.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “So that you may reason” can attach to “sent down,” or to “Arabic,” meaning it was made Arabic so its speakers could understand.
rows.anchor: تتعلق ب أنزلناه أي أنزلناه لعلكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Qur’an” is a circumstantial accusative and “Arabic” its adjective; alternatives make “Qur’an” apposition to the pronoun or a preparatory circumstantial noun.
rows.anchor: وقرآنا حال، وعربيا صفة له

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports the Companions tired and asked the Prophet for stories, prompting this verse; later they asked for a talk and al-Zumar 39:23 was revealed.
rows.anchor: روى ابن مسعود أن أصحاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ملوا ملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-qaṣaṣ means reporting events that happened, as accounts follow one another in speech and are recounted in succession.
rows.anchor: والقصص: الإخبار بما جرى من الأمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “By what We revealed” means by Our revelation; “the Qur’an” describes “this,” with apposition also possible and explanatory coordination judged weak.
rows.anchor: وقوله: بما أوحينا إليك أي بوحينا. والقرآن نعت ل هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basrans take lightened inna as a weakened emphatic particle and the lām as emphasis; Kufans read in as “not” and the lām as “except.”
rows.anchor: وإن هي المخففة من الثقيلة واللام في خبرها لام التأكيد- هذا مذهب البصريين- ومذهب أهل الكوفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Before it” refers to the general body of Qur’anic stories, and “unaware” means unaware of this story.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قبله للقصص العام لما في جميع القرآن منه. ومن الغافلين، أي عن معرفة هذا القصص.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “before it” refers to the Qur’an, “unaware” echoes 93:7: Muhammad sought guidance and was not among unbelievers or polytheists; Arabic calls a seeker uncertain of the way “lost.”
rows.anchor: جعل من الغافلين في معنى قوله تعالى: ووجدك ضالا فهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The temporal “when” has an omitted governing verb, understood as “remember”; it may depend on “We recount” in 12:3, while Makki’s link to “unaware” is weak.
rows.anchor: تقديره: اذكر إذ ويصح أن يعمل فيه نقص [يوسف: 3]

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa reads the name يوسف with hamza and fatḥa on its sīn; six forms are reported across hamza and vowel variants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة بن مصرف «يوسف» بالهمز وفتح السين

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: The majority read “my father” with kasra on the tā; Sībawayh says the yā of “my father” was deleted and replaced by tā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «يا أبت» بكسر التاء حذفت الياء من أبي

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأبو جعفر والأعرج
rows.claim: These readers use fatḥa on the tā; Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir pause on it with hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وحده وأبو جعفر والأعرج: «يا أبت» بفتحها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir’s fatḥa can preserve a deleted vocative alif, or reflect a diminutive form whose marker is restored after truncation.
rows.anchor: فأما قراءة ابن عامر بفتح التاء فلها وجهان

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر والحسن وطلحة بن سليمان
rows.claim: They read “eleven stars” with the ʿayn of ʿashar still to avoid successive vowels; the number words appear fused.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر والحسن وطلحة بن سليمان: «أحد عشر كوكبا» بسكون العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority say Joseph saw real stars, the sun, and moon, which Jacob interpreted as his brothers and parents.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه قد رأى كواكب حقيقة والشمس والقمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies them as Joseph’s brothers, father, and maternal aunt, since his mother had died.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الإخوة والأب والخالة لأن أمه كانت ميتة

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī frames the alternative that Joseph saw his family directly and represented them as stars; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak, as Qatāda’s and al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s reports are equivocal.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف ترجم به الطبري، ثم أدخل عن قتادة والضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes identify the moon as Joseph’s father and sun as his mother; some infer that a mother’s dutiful treatment takes precedence from the order.
rows.anchor: وقال المفسرون: القمر تأويله: الأب، والشمس تأويلها: الأم

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: A report says a Jew named Bustāna asked the Prophet for the stars’ names; after Gabriel informed him, the Prophet listed them and the questioner affirmed them.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن جابر بن عبد الله أن يهوديا يسمى بستانة جاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated “I saw them” lengthens the expression; the stars take rational masculine pronouns because they are described with rational actions.
rows.anchor: وتكرر رأيتهم لطول الكلام وجرى ضمائر هذه الكواكب في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports place Joseph’s dream on Laylat al-Qadr, a Friday night, and say it came true after forty or eighty years.
rows.anchor: وروي أن رؤيا يوسف كانت ليلة القدر ليلة جمعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob sensed envy and hatred in his sons; their later plan shows they were not prophets then, contrary to Ibn Zayd’s report, since such envy, filial disobedience, and plotting a believer’s death violate prophetic protection.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا ومن فعلهم بيوسف- الذي يأتي ذكره- يظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan is the manifest enemy who draws the brothers into this conduct and urges them toward it.
rows.anchor: أي هو يدخلهم في ذلك ويحضهم عليه

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī uses imāla for “your dream” and “dream”; another report says he leaves imāla on “your dream” in this sūra only.
rows.anchor: وأمال الكسائي رؤياك، والرؤيا حيث وقعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading without hamza, ruyāk, is Hejazi; the remaining readers do not use imāla on the word wherever it occurs.
rows.anchor: وقرأ «روياك» بغير همز- وهي لغة أهل الحجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruʾyā began as a verbal noun but frequent use for dreams made it a noun; its plural ruʾan follows ẓulum, though verbal nouns are seldom pluralized.
rows.anchor: و «الرؤيا» مصدر كثر وقوعه على هذا المتخيل في النوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yajtabī means choose or select, with the image of gathering water in a basin and the related term for collecting taxes.
rows.anchor: وقوله: وكذلك يجتبيك الآية، ف يجتبيك معناه: يختارك

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Suddī explain “interpretation of reports” as interpretation of dreams.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد والسدي: هي عبارة الرؤيا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan explains “interpretation of reports” as the outcomes of events.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هي عواقب الأمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view takes the phrase generally to cover dreams, outcomes, and other hidden matters.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي عامة لذلك وغيره من المغيبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Completing the blessing means prophethood and its accompanying gifts; Jacob’s family here means his descendants and kin, in whom prophethood would continue.
rows.anchor: وقوله: آل يعقوب يريد في هذا الموضع الأولاد والقرابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says Jacob knew this through Isaac’s prayer for him when he impersonated Esau; Ibn ʿAṭiyya abridges it as poorly worded and likely borrowed from Israelite books.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن ذلك إنما علمه يعقوب من دعوة إسحاق له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s blessings included prison rescue, protection, and kingship; Abraham’s was friendship with God, and Isaac’s redemption by the great sacrifice, all alongside prophethood.
rows.anchor: و «النعمة» على يوسف كانت تخليصه من السجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Knowing” and “wise” suit the promise of these blessings.
rows.anchor: وعليم حكيم مناسبتان لهذا الوعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers have plural “signs”; Ibn Kathīr alone with Mujāhid, Shibl, and Meccan readers has singular: each episode is a sign in the plural reading, while the whole story is one sign in the singular.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور «آيات» بالجمع، وقرأ ابن كثير- وحده- «آية»

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says a non-ʿUthmānic codex reads “a lesson for those who ask”; Abū Ḥātim says this wording is in Ubayy’s codex.
rows.anchor: وذكر الزجاج: أن في غير مصحف عثمان: «عبرة للسائلين»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the audience questioners urges learning these accounts, which are a source of lessons; it may identify them by the question that occasioned the sūra.
rows.anchor: وقوله: للسائلين يقتضي حضا ما على تعلم هذه الأنباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “His brother” means Yāmīn, younger than Joseph and also called Benjamin; they may have been full brothers because their mother died, though the grammar is not conclusive.
rows.anchor: وقولهم: وأخوه يريدون به: يامين- وهو أصغر من يوسف-

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s affection for Joseph and Benjamin reflects their youth and their mother’s death, an ordinary attachment illustrated by al-Ḥasan’s daughter’s saying one favors the youngest, absent, or sick child.
rows.anchor: وكان حب يعقوب ليوسف عليه السلام ويامين لصغرهما وموت أمهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUṣba means a group able to help, harm, protect, or abandon; proposed sizes range from ten–fifteen or ten–forty to around ten, while al-Zahrawī gives a taxonomy from three to over nine.
rows.anchor: و «العصبة» في اللغة: الجماعة، قيل: من عشرة إلى خمسة عشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Manifest error” means an evident mistake or partiality in loving Joseph and his brother; its seriousness depends on what it concerns.
rows.anchor: وقولهم: لفي ضلال مبين أي لفي اختلاف وخطأ في محبة

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر وحمزة
rows.claim: These readers kasr the tanwīn in “manifest error—kill” when joining the words, resolving two still consonants.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر وحمزة «مبين اقتلوا» بكسر التنوين

rows.speaker: نافع وابن كثير والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers kasr the nūn and give the tanwīn a ḍamma to follow the tāʾ’s ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن كثير والكسائي «مبين اقتلوا» بكسر النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kill Joseph” is some brothers’ proposal; “cast him away” means remove him, as in ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward’s line about casting oneself wherever needed.
rows.anchor: أو اطرحوه معناه: أبعدوه، ومنه قول عروة بن الورد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “To a land” is a second object with an omitted preposition, since ṭaraḥa takes two objects only that way; an adverb reading fails because this land is specified as distant, not vague.
rows.anchor: وأرضا مفعول ثان بإسقاط حرف الجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Your father’s face will be free for you” metaphorically means his affection will return when Joseph is gone, like the saying that bereavement softens a mother.
rows.anchor: وقوله: يخل لكم وجه أبيكم استعارة، أي إذا فقد يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “After him” can refer to Joseph, his killing, or his removal.
rows.anchor: والضمير في بعده عائد على يوسف أو قتله أو طرحه

rows.speaker: السدي ومقاتل بن سليمان
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and Muqātil take promised righteousness to mean setting matters right with their father; this fits their immediate intention, and they were not prophets then.
rows.anchor: وصالحين قال السدي ومقاتل بن سليمان: إنهم أرادوا صلاح الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority’s interpretation of “righteous” as repentance is more evident: believers commit a grave wrong and console themselves with future repentance.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور: صالحين معناه بالتوبة، وهذا هو الأظهر من اللفظ

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Qatāda and Ibn Isḥāq identify the protective speaker as Reuben, the eldest brother.
rows.anchor: القائل منهم قيل: هو روبيل- أسنهم- قاله قتادة وابن إسحاق

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the speaker as Simeon, the bravest brother.
rows.anchor: وقيل شمعون أشجعهم، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies Judah, the most forbearing; whoever spoke was protective of his brother, and God’s decree would proceed.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يهوذا أحلمهم، وقيل شمعون أشجعهم، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ghiyāba is a place hidden from view or one that hides something from you.
rows.anchor: و «الغيابة» ما غاب عنك من الأماكن أو غيب عنك شيئا آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya questions comparing ghiyāba with the examples because ghiyāba follows the form fiʿl.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وفي شبه غيابة بهذه الأمثلة نظر

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads ghayba on the pattern fiʿla; it is also written that way in Ubayy’s codex, and al-Munakhkhal’s poem uses ghiyābati for absence.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن: «في غيبة الجب» على وزن فعلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A jubb is a well dug into the ground without being lined.
rows.anchor: والجب البئر التي لم تطو لأنها جبت من الأرض فقط.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read yaltaqiṭ-hu with masculine yāʾ agreeing with baʿḍ; al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and Abū Rajāʾ use feminine tāʾ by association with the feminine collective sayyāra, with poetic support.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: «يلتقطه بعض» بالياء من تحت على لفظ بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Bedouins found Joseph; sayyāra is an intensive form for a traveling party. The well is variously located at Jerusalem or elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وروي أن جماعة من الأعراب التقطت يوسف عليه السلام: والسيارة جمع سيار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports differ on the well: it may have been dry, with God directing travelers to draw water there, or flooded until a stone rose beneath Joseph and held him up.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لم يكن حيث طرحوه ماء ولكن أخرجه الله فيه حتى قصده الناس للاستقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the brothers lowered Joseph by rope; he held on, was bound and stripped, and they wanted to stone him until the brother who proposed the well stopped them.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهم رموه بحبل في الجب فتماسك بيديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers’ plea implies their father already knew their malicious intent toward Joseph, and they knew that he knew.
rows.anchor: الآية الأولى تقتضي أن أباهم قد كان علم منهم إرادتهم الخبيثة

rows.speaker: الزهري وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī and Abū Jaʿfar read “trust us” with full assimilation and no imāla; seven readers use imāla, while Ṭalḥa and Ibn Wathāb with al-Aʿmash have other forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري وأبو جعفر «لا تأمنا» بالإدغام دون إشمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghadā originally meant morning but came to mean the whole following day; ghudū and ghudwa remain names for early day, with al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl defining ghudwa as dawn to first light.
rows.anchor: وغدا ظرف أصله: غدو، فلزم اليوم كله

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وأبو عامر
rows.claim: They read “we graze and play” in first-person plural; ritaʿ means staying in fertile pasture and eating and drinking abundantly, supported by poetry.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وأبو عامر: «نرتع ونلعب» بالنون فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their play could be permissible activities such as riding and archery, not frivolity; Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ says they were not prophets then.
rows.anchor: و «لعبهم» هذا دخل في اللعب المباح كاللعب بالخيل والرمي ونحوه

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads “we graze, he plays” in a report; ritaʿ can mean tending camels, while Mujāhid says it means watching one another.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير: «نرتع ونلعب» بالنون فيهما، وبكسر العين

rows.speaker: عاصم وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read “he grazes and plays,” assigning both activities to Joseph.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم وحمزة والكسائي «يرتع ويلعب» بإسناد ذلك كله إلى يوسف

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ reads “he grazes” with yāʾ and “plays” jussive; the verb refers to tending livestock.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع «يرتع» بالياء فيهما وكسر العين وجزم الباء

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the reading refers to Joseph training in herding and caring for property; al-Aʿshā’s line with ترتعي supports the grazing sense.
rows.anchor: ف «يرتع» - على هذا- من رعي الإبل قال ابن زيد: المعنى:

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī favors Ibn Kathīr’s “we graze, he plays”: the brothers tend the property and Joseph, being young, plays.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: وقراءة ابن كثير- «نرتع» بالنون و «يلعب» بالياء- فنزعها حسن

rows.speaker: العلاء بن سيابة
rows.claim: Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Siyāba reads yartʿu wayalʿab with the bāʾ indicative after a break.
rows.anchor: وقرأ العلاء بن سيابة، «يرتع ويلعب» برفع الباء على القطع

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda read nartaʿ with ḍamma on nūn and kasra on tāʾ, followed by nalʿab in the jussive.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وقتادة: «نرتع» بضم النون وكسر التاء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Some transmissions retain final yāʾ in nartaʿī; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it weak and permissible only in poetry, citing ألم يأتيك.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير- في بعض الروايات عنه- «نرتعي» بإثبات الياء

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abū Rajāʾ reads yartaʿ with ḍamma on yāʾ and jussive ʿayn, and yalʿab with yāʾ and a jussive ending.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء «يرتع» بضم الياء وجزم العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers framed their request around grazing, play, and activity likely to appeal to Joseph as a child.
rows.anchor: وعللوا طلبه والخروج به بما يمكن أن يستهوي يوسف لصباه

rows.speaker: عاصم وابن كثير والحسن والأعرج وعيسى وأبو عمرو وابن محيصن
rows.claim: These readers pronounce “grieve me” with fatḥa on yāʾ and ḍamma on zāy; Nāfiʿ has a variant with ḍamma yāʾ, kasra zāy, and assimilation.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم وابن كثير والحسن والأعرج وعيسى وأبو عمرو وابن محيصن «ليحزنني» بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ’s reported reading uses ḍamma on the first yāʾ and kasra on zāy with assimilation; Warsh distinguishes two nūns, first active and second object of “I fear.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع بضم الياء وكسر الزاي والإدغام

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī reads dhīb without hamza; the hamza is standard, reflected in the plural dhiʾbān and verb for a shifting wind.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي وحده: «الذيب» دون همز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob named the wolf because it was the familiar predator in his region; his reported wolf dream is weak because a prophetic dream would need fulfillment or clear interpretation.
rows.anchor: وإنما خاف يعقوب الذئب دون سواه، وخصصه لأنه كان الحيوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wolf-dream explanation remains remote even if Jacob feared an analogous event; he may have chosen a seemingly weak animal because Joseph was small, like the poet al-Rabīʿ ibn Ḍabʿ.
rows.anchor: وهذا بعيد- وكذلك يقول الربيع بن ضبع: [المنسرح] والذئب أخشاه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the brothers first treated Joseph honorably, then beat and threatened him in the open country; Judah stopped them killing him, but they tied him, stripped him, dropped him into the well, where he stood on a rock and cried. Judah prevented stoning him and brought food.
rows.anchor: أسند الطبري إلى السدي قال: ذهبوا بيوسف وبه عليهم كرامة

rows.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
rows.claim: They take the response to “when they took him and agreed” as an omitted repeated verb: “when they took him, they resolved”; Imruʾ al-Qays and 37:103 give similar constructions.
rows.anchor: وجواب «لما» محذوف تقديره: فلما ذهبوا به وأجمعوا أجمعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians call the wāw redundant, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this because nothing in the Qur’an is redundant without meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض النحاة- في مثل هذا-: إن الواو زائدة- وقوله مردود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ajmaʿū means resolve and agree; the Prophet’s saying about a traveler uses it for an individual’s resolve or start to settle, while collective usage may lack a firm decision or start.
rows.anchor: وأجمعوا معناه: عزموا واتفق رأيهم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “We revealed to him” most correctly and commonly refers to Joseph; another view refers to Jacob.
rows.anchor: والضمير في إليه عائد إلى يوسف. وقيل على يعقوب، والأول أصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation to Joseph may have come through a messenger, inspiration, or a dream.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون الوحي حينئذ إلى يوسف برسول

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says God granted Joseph prophethood in the well; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls that remote.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: أعطاه الله النبوءة وهو في الجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use second-person tāʾ in “you will inform them”; some Basran codices have yāʾ, while Salām reads nūn after the lām.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: «لتنبئنهم» بالتاء، وفي بعض مصاحف البصرة بالياء

rows.speaker: ابن جريح
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj takes “while they do not perceive” to mean that the brothers will not recognize Joseph when he later informs them of their deed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جريح: وقت التنبيه إنك يوسف

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes the phrase to mean that the brothers do not perceive the revelation given to Joseph.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: لا يشعرون بوحينا إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first interpretation, the phrase is part of what Joseph was told; on Qatāda’s reading it is information addressed to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: فيكون قوله: وهم لا يشعرون- على التأويل الأول- مما أوحي إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says the caravan arrived the day after Joseph was cast into the well; sayyāra is intensive for repeated road travelers, and the group is identified as Midianites or Bedouins.
rows.anchor: قيل إن «السيارة» جاءت في اليوم الثاني من طرحه في الجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wā rid goes to water for a group; the drawer is reported as Mālik ibn Dhʿr, and the well is placed in Jordan three farsakhs from Jacob’s home.
rows.anchor: و «الوارد» هو الذي يأتي الماء ليسقي منه لجماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adlā al-dalwa means lowering the bucket into the well; dalā yadlūhu means drawing water out. The narrative omits Joseph grasping the rope and the drawer’s exclamation.
rows.anchor: ويقال: «أدلى الدلو» : إذا ألقاه في البئر ليستقي الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph is reported to have been seven, which suits ghulām as boy from age two until puberty; the report that he was seventeen is unlikely.
rows.anchor: وروي أن يوسف كان يومئذ ابن سبع سنين

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers make “my good news” a vocative with possessive yāʾ: “O glad tidings, come, for this is your moment,” like 36:30.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر «يا بشراي» بإضافة البشرى

rows.speaker: ورش
rows.claim: Warsh reports a still yāʾ; Abū ʿAlī allows two still consonants because alif has extra length not shared by yāʾ and wāw.
rows.anchor: وروى ورش عن نافع «يا بشراي» بسكون الياء

rows.speaker: أبو الطفيل والجحدري وابن أبي إسحاق والحسن
rows.claim: They convert alif to yāʾ and assimilate it into the possessive yāʾ, a widespread dialectal form supported by Abū Dhuʾayb’s verse.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو الطفيل والجحدري وابن أبي إسحاق والحسن «يا بشري»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-Fatḥ and others cite additional lines attesting the assimilated yāʾ reading of bushrāy.
rows.anchor: وأنشد أبو الفتح وغيره في ذلك: يطوف بي كعب في معد

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read bushrāy without possessive addition and with imāla; ʿĀṣim omits possessive addition but opens rāʾ without imāla.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي «يا بشري» ويميلان ولا يضيفان

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says a man named Bushrā was in the drawer’s party and was being called; another view makes the call a personification of glad tidings.
rows.anchor: فقال السدي: كان في أصحاب هذا «الوارد» رجل اسمه بشرى

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid assigns “they concealed him” to the water drawer, who hid Joseph lest caravan traders claim a share.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله: وأسروه ظاهر الآيات أنه ل «وارد» الماء، - قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concealment could reflect corrupt intent or fear honest travelers would prevent ownership; they planned to claim a townsman entrusted him as merchandise.
rows.anchor: فأسروا بينهم أن يقولوا: أبضعه معنا بعض أهل المصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Biḍāʿa is a circumstantial accusative: capital traded without a profit share, from a root meaning “I cut.”
rows.anchor: وبضاعة حال، و «البضاعة» : القطعة من المال يتجر فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, they hid their own plan to make Joseph merchandise, then sold him cheaply because they did not know his worth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم أسروا في أنفسهم يتخذونه بضاعة لأنفسهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid assigns the pronoun in “they concealed him” to the water-drawers and the one in “they sold him” to Joseph’s brothers.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: الضمير في أسروه لأصحاب «الدلو» ، وفي شروه لإخوة يوسف الأحد عشر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās assigns both pronouns in “they concealed him” and “they sold him” to the brothers.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: بل الضمير في أسروه وشروه لإخوة يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers returned to verify Joseph’s fate, claimed he was their mother’s runaway slave, and sold him; he went along in fear so God’s plan could unfold.
rows.anchor: فقالوا: هذا عبد أبق لأمنا ووهبته لنا ونحن نبيعه منكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God knows what they do” threatens the brothers if they are meant, or signals divine direction of events for Joseph if the caravan is meant.
rows.anchor: إن كانت الضمائر لإخوة يوسف ففي ذلك توعد، وإن كانت الضمائر للواردين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode consoles Muhammad regarding Quraysh: the expected outcome for the God-fearing is care and vindication.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية- أيضا- تسلية للنبي عليه السلام عما يجري عليه من جهة قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here shara means “sold,” though the root can mean “bought”; Yazīd ibn Mufarrigh’s cloak-selling verse illustrates this use.
rows.anchor: وشروه- هنا- بمعنى باعوه، وقد يقال: شرى، بمعنى اشترى

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī takes bakhs as reduction; Qatāda says injustice, while al-Ḍaḥḥāk says unlawful, a sense al-Zajjāj prefers because a free person cannot lawfully be sold.
rows.anchor: «البخس» مصدر وصف به «الثمن» وهو بمعنى النقص- وهذا أشهر معانيه- فكأنه القليل الناقص- وهو قول الشعبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Counted dirhams” signals a small price: sums below an uqiyya of forty dirhams were counted rather than weighed.
rows.anchor: وقوله: دراهم معدودة عبارة عن قلة الثمن لأنها دراهم لم تبلغ أن توزن

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Prices are reported as ten, twenty according to Ibn Masʿūd, twenty-two according to Mujāhid with two taken by the brothers, or forty underweight dirhams according to ʿIkrima.
rows.anchor: واختلف في مبلغ ثمن يوسف عليه السلام: فقيل باعوه بعشرة دراهم، وقال ابن مسعود: بعشرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They disdained him” may describe the water-drawers’ ignorance, but fits the brothers better because they truly rejected Joseph; the traders’ holding him for sale is only figuratively disdainful.
rows.anchor: لكنه أرتب في إخوة يوسف إذ حقيقة الزهد في الشيء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says fīhi is not governed by “disdained”; Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects that this makes them generally ascetic rather than specifically disdainful of Joseph.
rows.anchor: وقوله فيه ليست بصلة ل الزاهدين- قاله الزجاج وفيه نظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports say the buyer brought Joseph to Egypt, displayed him in the market, and bought him after bidding rose greatly; he was the king’s chamberlain and treasurer.
rows.anchor: روي أن مبتاع يوسف- وهو الوارد من إخوته أو التاجر من الوراد، حسبما تقدم من الخلاف- ورد به مصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king is named Rayyān ibn al-Walīd or Muṣʿab ibn al-Rayān; the claim that this was Moses’ Pharaoh who lived until then is called weak.
rows.anchor: واسم الملك الريان بن الوليد، وقيل مصعب بن الريان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās names the Aziz Quṭfīr; other forms are Quṭūr or Aṭfīr. His wife is Raʿīl according to Ibn Isḥāq, or Rabīḥa or Zulaykhā.
rows.anchor: واسم العزيز المذكور: قطفير، قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The Aziz appears to be a disbeliever because an idol was in his house; Mujāhid says he was Muslim.
rows.anchor: وظاهر أمر العزيز أنه كان كافرا، ويدل على ذلك كون الصنم في بيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathwā means residence; honoring the place figuratively honors its resident. The buyer hoped Joseph would help them or be adopted as a son because he had no child.
rows.anchor: و «المثوى» مكان الإقامة، و «الإكرام» إنما هو لذي المثوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Likewise” means God enabled Joseph in the land and did so to teach him the interpretation of reports.
rows.anchor: ثم قال تعالى: وكذلك، أي كما وصفنا مكنا ليوسف في الأرض

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets “reports” as dreams; another view takes them as accounts of peoples and prophets.
rows.anchor: والأحاديث: الرؤيا في النوم- قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: الطبري وابن جبير
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī refers the pronoun in “His affair” to Joseph; Ibn Jubayr refers it to God, making the statement about general divine power.
rows.anchor: قاله الطبري، ويحتمل أن يعود على الله عز وجل، قاله ابن جبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem about Abū Bakr says God is master over His affair, illustrating the pronoun’s possible reference to God.
rows.anchor: رأيت أبا بكر- وربك- غالب ... على أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those said not to know are mainly unbelievers, including those who undervalued Joseph and others ignorant of his destiny.
rows.anchor: وأكثر الناس الذين نفي عنهم العلم هم الكفرة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd names three people of exceptional insight: the Aziz, Shuʿayb’s daughter in 28:26, and Abū Bakr when appointing ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عبد الله بن مسعود أنه قال: أصح الناس فراسة ثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Aziz perceived only Joseph’s noble character; unlike the other two examples, his foresight did not exactly predict the outcome.
rows.anchor: وفراسة العزيز إنما كانت في نفس نجابة يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ashudd means full strength: it begins at puberty according to Mālik and Rabīʿa; common usage may extend from eighteen to sixty, which Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls weak.
rows.anchor: و «الأشد» : استكمال القوة وتناهي البأس، أولهما البلوغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other thresholds are forty, thirty-six, thirty-three, or twenty; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers thirty-three and calls twenty weak.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا هو أظهر الأقوال- فيما نحسبه- وهو الأسبوع الخامس

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says ashudd has no singular; Sībawayh derives it from shidda, al-Kisāʾī from shadd, meaning the day’s culmination.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: «الأشد» لا واحد له من لفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥukm may be wisdom and prophethood, wisdom and knowledge without prophethood (more likely if the seduction occurred later), or worldly authority and judging rightly; knowledge includes dream interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقوله: حكما يحتمل أن يريد الحكمة والنبوءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Thus We reward the excellent” promises Muhammad that God will deal well with the righteous despite unbelievers’ persecution and defiance.
rows.anchor: وكذلك نجزي المحسنين ألفاظ فيها وعد للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Murāwada is gentle coaxing toward an aim, especially between men and women; it may derive from testing land or pasture, as the coaxer tests willingness through tactful speech.
rows.anchor: «المراودة» الملاطفة في السوق إلى غرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woman was Zulaykhā; “about himself” euphemizes intercourse, and the intensified ghallaqat emphasizes closing the doors rather than making the verb causative.
rows.anchor: والتي هو في بيتها هي زليخا امرأة العزيز. وقوله عن نفسه كناية عن غرض المواقعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode apparently occurred before Joseph became a prophet.
rows.anchor: وظاهر هذه النازلة أنها كانت قبل أن ينبأ عليه السلام.

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأهل مكة
rows.claim: They read hayta with fatḥa on hāʾ, still yāʾ, and ḍamma on tāʾ; other readers have forms with kasra or fatḥa on tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأهل مكة: «هيت» بفتح الهاء وسكون الياء وضم التاء

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read hayta with kasra on hāʾ, still yāʾ, and fatḥa on tāʾ; the principal forms all mean “come, approach.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن عامر «هيت» بكسر الهاء وسكون الياء وفتح التاء

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says hayta means halumma, “come”; lak attaches to an implied verbal noun such as “approach.”
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: معناها هلم، ويحسن أن تتصل بها لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic examples by an unnamed poet addressing the Commander of the Faithful, Ṭarafa, and another poet attest hayta as an utterance, like saying “alas” or “glorify.”
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك على اللغة الأخرى قول طرفة: [الخفيف] ليس قومي بالأبعدين

rows.speaker: هشام ابن عامر
rows.claim: Hishām reads hīʾta with kasra and hamza on hāʾ and ḍamma on tāʾ; it may mean making oneself ready or “I made ready.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ هشام ابن عامر «هيت» ، بكسر الهاء والهمز، ضم التاء

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Isḥāq also reads a facilitated hamza; al-Ḥulwānī’s alternative is judged an error by Abū ʿAlī because syntax would require lī rather than lak.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي إسحاق- أيضا- «هيت» بتسهيل الهمزة

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās records a further reading with kasra on hāʾ, still yāʾ, and kasra on tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وحكى النحاس: أنه يقرأ «هيت» بكسر الهاء وسكون الياء وكسر التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿādh is an accusative verbal noun meaning “I seek refuge in God.”
rows.anchor: ومعاذ نصب على المصدر ومعنى الكلام أعوذ بالله.

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: They take “He is my lord” to mean the Aziz, Joseph’s master; the pronoun could instead refer to God, and Joseph must not betray a host who honored him.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد، والسدي ربي معناه سيدي، وقاله ابن إسحاق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Honoring a human for kindness is virtuous; honoring God is all the more incumbent.
rows.anchor: وإذا حفظ الآدمي لإحسانه فهو عمل زاك، وأحرى أن يحفظ ربه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “He is my lord” may refer to the situation, after which “my lord treated me well” begins anew; the pronoun in “he does not prosper” is likewise an idiom for the situation.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون الضمير للأمر والشأن، ثم يبتدىء ربي أحسن مثواي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpreters say Joseph gently argued after seeking refuge and was tested with desire; they speculate a forceful refusal invoking God would prevent inclination.
rows.anchor: وحكى بعض المفسرين: أن يوسف عليه الصلاة والسلام- لما قال: معاذ الله

rows.speaker: الجحدري وأبو طفيل
rows.claim: Al-Jaḥdarī and Abū Ṭufayl read mathwāy; a prophetic quotation of “whoever follows My guidance” is also cited.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجحدري «مثواي» وقرأها كذلك أبو طفيل

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reports a view that Joseph’s desire matched hers; proponents explain it as a lesson in forgiveness and repentance and describe a physical intention, citing Ibn ʿAbbās and others.
rows.anchor: فقال الطبري: قالت فرقة: كان مثل «همها»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another group says Joseph’s himma was an involuntary passing thought from which he turned back; they cite reports rewarding an unacted evil thought, with one or ten good deeds.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة في «همه» إنما كان بخطرات القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group says Joseph’s himma meant intending to strike her; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this outright.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: كان «هم» يوسف بضربها ونحو ذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s prophethood then is unproven. As a believer he could intend without acting; if already a prophet, only a fleeting thought is possible, not undressing or similar conduct.
rows.anchor: والذي أقول في هذه الآية: إن كون يوسف نبيا في وقت هذه النازلة لم يصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A passing inclination may occur even to a prophet, but indulging a sinful thought with pleasure is itself a sin; the report about a future prophetic register concerns later prophethood.
rows.anchor: والهم بالشيء مرتبتان: فالواحدة الأولى تجوز عليه مع النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pardon for unspoken thoughts concerns fleeting thoughts, not sustained indulgence; the hadith about eagerness to kill a companion and 49:12 on sinful suspicion support the distinction.
rows.anchor: وقول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إن الله تجاوز لأمتي ما حدثت به نفوسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Consensus holds that sustained intention and pleasure in sin are impermissible and outside the pardon for passing thoughts.
rows.anchor: والإجماع منعقد أن الهم بالمعصية واستصحاب التلذذ بها غير جائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explanations of Joseph’s proof include divine calls by Gabriel or Jacob warning against sin, a written text on a wall or between Zulaykhā’s eyes, or words appearing in a hand; proposed texts include 13:33 and 17:32.
rows.anchor: واختلف في «البرهان» الذي رأى يوسف، وقيل: نودي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports show Jacob biting his thumb or lip, the ceiling opening to reveal him, or Gabriel threatening to remove Joseph from the prophetic register.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان «البرهان» كتابا رآه مكتوبا، فقيل: في جدار المجلس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report that Gabriel kicked Joseph and desire emerged through his fingertips is called weak.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن جبريل ركضه فخرجت شهوته على أنامله. قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proofs are reflection on God’s punishment or Joseph’s lesson when Zulaykhā covered her idol from shame: he should be more ashamed before God, who sees all.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بل كان البرهان الذي اتعظ به أن زليخا قالت له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Burhān is anything giving certainty through necessary knowledge, conclusive report, or reasoning; the listed accounts are explanations of what Joseph saw.
rows.anchor: و «البرهان» في كلام العرب الشيء الذي يعطي القطع واليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “if he had not seen his Lord’s proof,” the clause is nominal and means “if not for his seeing”; the omitted result is that he would have committed the sin.
rows.anchor: وأن في قوله: لولا أن رأى في موضع رفع، التقدير: لولا رؤيته برهان ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some make “he would have desired her” the result of “if not for the proof,” but Arabic and early authorities reject this syntax; al-Zajjāj says even an explicit lām would be awkward.
rows.anchor: وذهب قوم إلى أن الكلام تم في قوله: ولقد همت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf in “thus” can depend on an omitted phrase about God’s acts and decrees, or be nominative for His protection of Joseph.
rows.anchor: والكاف من قوله: كذلك متعلقة بمضمر تقديره: جرت أفعالنا وأقدارنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read “to turn away” with nūn; al-Aʿmash reads yāʾ as narration about an absent subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «لنصرف» بالنون، وقرأ الأعمش «ليصرف» بالياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والحسن وأبو رجاء
rows.claim: These readers kasr the lām in mukhliṣīn throughout; Nāfiʿ does so in specified verses, while others use fatḥa in remaining forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والحسن بن أبي الحسن وأبو رجاء «المخلصين» بكسر اللام

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وجمهور القراء
rows.claim: These readers use fatḥa on the lām in mukhliṣīn and mukhliṣan throughout the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وجمهور من القراء «المخلصين» بفتح اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They raced to the door: she sought to draw Joseph back, while he fled; she seized his shirt from behind and tore it lengthwise from collar to hem.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: واستبقا الباب الآية، واستبقا معناه سابق كل واحد منهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qadd is usually a lengthwise cut and qaṭṭ crosswise, supported by al-Nābigha’s verse.
rows.anchor: و «القد» : القطع، وأكثر ما يستعمل فيما كان طولا، «والقط» يستعمل فيما كان عرضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alfayā means “found,” and sayyid means husband according to Zayd ibn Thābit and Mujāhid.
rows.anchor: وألفيا: وجدا، و «السيد» الزوج، قاله زيد بن ثابت ومجاهد.

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says they found the Aziz and a male relative of Zulaykhā at the door.
rows.anchor: فيروى أنهما وجدا العزيز ورجلا من قرابة زليخا عند الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Frightened by exposure, Zulaykhā accused Joseph and spoke of punishment as if guilt were established.
rows.anchor: فلما رأت الفضيحة فزعت إلى مطالبة يوسف والبغي عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shows how severe imprisonment is to people’s spirits, especially those of high standing, since it is paired with painful punishment.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية تقتضي بعظم موقع السجن من النفوس لا سيما بذوي الأقدار

rows.speaker: نوف الشامي
rows.claim: Nawf al-Shāmī says Joseph had not exposed the affair, but when Zulaykhā falsely accused him he became angry and told the truth.
rows.anchor: قال نوف الشامي: كان يوسف عليه السلام لم يبن على كشف القصة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī identifies the witness as the woman’s male cousin, who proposed checking whether Joseph’s shirt was torn in front or behind.
rows.anchor: فروي أن الشاهد كان الرجل ابن عمها، قال: انظر إلى القميص

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وغيرهما
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and others identify the witness as a man from the king’s inner circle.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كان رجلا من خاصة الملك، قاله مجاهد وغيره.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو هريرة وابن جبير وهلال بن يساف والضحاك
rows.claim: They identify the witness as a speaking infant; Ibn ʿAṭiyya weakens this because Bukhārī and Muslim name only three cradle-speakers, and the infant’s words alone would prove the case.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الشاهد كان طفلا في المهد فتكلم بهذا، قاله أيضا ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet said four spoke in the cradle, adding Joseph’s witness; another report makes Pharaoh’s hairdresser’s son a fifth.
rows.anchor: وأسند الطبري إلى ابن عباس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «تكلم في المهد أربعة»

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the witness was the shirt; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak because a shirt is not one of the family.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد- أيضا- الشاهد القميص. قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read “in front” and “behind” with ḍamma and tanwīn; another reading builds them as adverbs, which Abū Ḥātim calls very poor Arabic. Other readers report forms with still bāʾ or unmarked endings.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس: «من قبل» و «من دبر» بضم الباءين وبالتنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speaker is called witness because he indicated the evidence; the shirt’s tear is the actual proof.
rows.anchor: وسمي المتكلم بهذا الكلام شاهد من حيث دل على الشاهد ونفس الشاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group reads “when he saw his shirt torn from behind” with ʿaṭṭ; al-Ṭabarī makes the Aziz say “it is your scheme,” while another view gives the words to the witness.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة: «فلما رأى قميصه عط من دبر» .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “it is your scheme” refers to Zulaykhā’s preceding accusation.
rows.anchor: والضمير في إنه يريد مقالها المتقدم في الشكوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jurists who allow judgment from circumstantial signs rely on this verse’s shirt evidence.
rows.anchor: ونزع بهذه الآية من يرى الحكم بالأمارة، من العلماء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās takes “Joseph” as a vocative by the witness, the man with the Aziz; “turn away from this” means stop discussing it.
rows.anchor: ويوسف في قوله: يوسف أعرض عن هذا منادى، قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The witness tells Zulaykhā to seek forgiveness from her husband and master.
rows.anchor: ثم رجع إليها فقال: واستغفري لذنبك أي استغفري زوجك وسيدك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine plural “those who err” is broader than feminine plural; the author cites verses by Aws ibn Ghalfāʾ and Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt as usage evidence.
rows.anchor: وقال: من الخاطئين ولم يقل: من الخاطئات لأن الخاطئين أعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine verb with al-niswa reflects the collective noun; niswah is a feminine minor plural with no same-form singular, while nisāʾ is the major plural. A verse lists four short-count patterns.
rows.anchor: ذكر الفعل المسند إلى «النسوة» لتذكير اسم الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the women were four: a baker’s wife, water carrier’s wife, gatekeeper’s wife, and jailer’s wife.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن هؤلاء النسوة كن أربعا: امرأة خبازة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAzīz means king; fatā means young male servant or young person. A hadith recommends this respectful term over “my slave,” and the Qur’an uses it for Moses’ companion.
rows.anchor: والعزيز: الملك ومنه قول الشاعر: [الرمل]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shaghafah means love reached the shighāf, an outer heart membrane; others say the heart’s core or a disease reaching it.
rows.anchor: وشغفها معناه: بلغ حتى صار من قلبها موضع الشغاف

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء والأعرج وعلي بن أبي طالب والحسن ويحيى بن يعمر وقتادة وثابت وعوف ومجاهد
rows.claim: They read shaʿafah with unpointed ʿayn: either love elevated her above all heights, from mountain peaks, or it burned the heart like an irritating wound.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء والأعرج وعلي بن أبي طالب والحسن بخلاف ويحيى بن يعمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s line uses shaʿafah for scorching love; al-Aʿshā calls the lover al-mashʿūf, consumed by love.
rows.anchor: أيقتلني وقد شعفت فؤادها ... كما شعف المهنوءة الرجل الطالي

rows.speaker: ثابت البناني وأبو رجاء
rows.claim: They are reported to read shaʿafahumā with kasra on unpointed ʿayn; Abū Ḥātim says fatḥa is familiar but acknowledges this reading.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ثابت البناني وأبي رجاء أنهما قرآ: «قد شعفعما»

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin reads shaghafahā with assimilation of dāl into shīn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن: قد شغفها أدغم الدال في الشين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The women may have spoken to anger Zulaykhā into showing Joseph, so they could understand her excuse or vindicate their criticism.
rows.anchor: وروي أن مقالة هؤلاء النسوة إنما قصدن بها المكر بامرأة العزيز

rows.speaker: ابن زيد والشعبي
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says shaghaf can mean love or hatred; al-Shaʿbī distinguishes dotted ghayn for love from unpointed ʿayn for madness. Both views are called weak.
rows.anchor: وقد قال ابن زيد الشغف في الحب والشغف في البغض، وقال الشعبي:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their speech is called a trick because they outwardly condemned wrongdoing while aiming to provoke Zulaykhā; leaking a secret she entrusted would count as trickery only if they feigned the opposite and intended harm.
rows.anchor: إنما سمي قولهن مكرا من حيث أظهرن إنكار منكر وقصدن إثارة غيظها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arsalat means she summoned them; aʿtadat means prepared. Muttaka is something leaned on, figuratively a reception; such hospitality includes food and drink.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أرسلت إليهن أي ليحضرن، وأعتدت معناه: أعدت ويسرت

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة
rows.claim: They interpret muttaka as food; Ibn ʿAbbās says a gathering, and al-Qutaybī notes “we reclined at someone” can mean “we ate there.”
rows.anchor: فلذلك فسر مجاهد وعكرمة «المتكأ» بالطعام قال ابن عباس: متكأ معناه مجلسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The knives suggest meat, citron, or zammāward, a local sweet made from sugar, almonds, and other ingredients.
rows.anchor: وقوله: وآتت كل واحدة منهن سكينا يقتضي أنه كان في جملة الطعام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والجحدري وابن عمر وقتادة والضحاك والكلبي وأبان بن تغلب
rows.claim: They read mutkan with ḍamma on mīm and tanwīn on kāf; it may mean citron or fruit cut with a knife.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس ومجاهد والجحدري وابن عمر وقتادة والضحاك والكلبي وأبان بن تغلب «تكا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī cites a poetic line about drinking sin from a bowl and the borrowed mutak among diners, illustrating a term for knife-cut fruit or food.
rows.anchor: نشرب الإثم بالصواع جهارا ... وترى المتك بيننا مستعارا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read muttaka with doubled open tāʾ, hamza, and short vowel; al-Zuhrī and others omit hamza, while al-Ḥasan lengthens it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: «متكا» بشد التاء المفتوحة والهمز والقصر

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء والأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ say sikkīn can be masculine or feminine; al-Aṣmaʿī recognizes only masculine.
rows.anchor: و «السكين» تذكر وتؤنث، قاله الكسائي والفراء

rows.speaker: مكي والمهدوي
rows.claim: Makkī and al-Mahdawī suggest the women’s gathering preceded Zulaykhā’s shirt incident, making the narrative order nonchronological.
rows.anchor: وقال مكي والمهدوي: قيل: إن في الآية تقديما وتأخيرا في القصص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reordered chronology is possible but not required: the Aziz showed little jealousy, and after the shirt test may have ignored the matter because the sign was circumstantial unless the witness was an infant.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا محتمل إلا أنه لا يلزم من ألفاظ الآية

rows.speaker: عبد الصمد بن علي الهاشمي
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Ṣamad says akbarnahu means the women menstruated; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this meaning objectionable, its supporting poem fabricated, and the narrator unreliable in learning.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الصمد بن علي الهاشمي عن أبيه عن جده: معناه: حضن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority understand akbarnahu as greatly admiring Joseph and being overwhelmed by his beauty.
rows.anchor: وقوله: أكبرنه معناه: أعظمنه واستهولن جماله، هذا قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima interprets “their hands” as sleeves; Mujāhid says limbs, which they cut with knives.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: «الأيدي» هنا الأكمام، وقال مجاهد هي الجوارح
